t.1.2: On that mountain the lover, parted from his beloved, passed some months, his forearm bare from the slipping of his golden bracelet; then, on the first day of Āṣāḍha, he saw a cloud clinging to the summit, lovely to behold as an elephant bending in play to butt against a bank.
t.1.3: Standing somehow before that cloud, the cause of the stirring of longing, the follower of the king of kings, holding his tears within, brooded for a long while; at the sight of a cloud even a happy man's heart is moved otherwise, how much more when the one who yearns for the embrace of his neck dwells far away?
t.1.1: A certain Yakṣa, negligent of his own duty, had his greatness brought to its setting by his master's curse, a curse made heavy by separation from his beloved and to be endured for a year. He made his dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, among waters made holy by the bathing of Janaka's daughter and among trees of dense, cool shade.
t.1.5: Where is a cloud, a mere mingling of smoke, light, water and wind, and where are messages that must be carried by living beings with keen senses? Not weighing this in his eagerness, the Guhyaka entreated him, for those tormented by love are by their very nature pitiable in their pleading to the sentient and the insentient alike.
t.1.4: As the month of Nabhas drew near, he, longing to sustain his beloved's life and intending to have the cloud carry news of his own well-being, was pleased, and to that cloud, for whom he had prepared a guest-offering of fresh kuṭaja flowers, he spoke a welcome in words full of affection.
t.1.6: I know you, born in the world-renowned lineage of the Puṣkarāvartakas, the chief minister of Maghavan, able to take any form at will; therefore, parted from my kin by the power of fate, I have become a suppliant to you. Better a request that fails with one of high virtue than one that gains its wish from the base.
t.1.7: You are the refuge of those who are scorched, so, O cloud, carry my message to my beloved, for I have been parted from her by the wrath of the Lord of Wealth. You must go to the dwelling of the lords of the Yakṣas, named Alakā, whose mansions are washed by the moonlight from the moon on the head of Hara, who stands in its outer garden.
t.1.8: The wives of travelers, holding back the ends of their locks, will gaze at you as you mount the path of the wind, taking comfort from the assurance you bring. When you stand girded for the season, who would neglect a wife distraught with separation, unless he were someone like me, whose life is subject to another's will?
t.1.9: And you, your course unhindered, will surely see your brother's wife, faithful to one husband, intent on counting the days and still alive. For the bond of hope, as a rule, swiftly guards the loving heart of women, delicate as a flower, and holds it back from failing in separation.
t.1.10: As the favorable wind drives you on gently, gently, and this cātaka, your kinsman, sings sweetly on your left, surely the cranes, strung together in garlands and knowing you from the season of conception, will attend you in the sky, you who are a delight to the eyes.
t.1.12: Embrace this lofty mountain, your dear friend, and take leave of him, whose slopes are marked with the footprints of Raghupati, worthy of men's reverence, and whose affection shows itself season after season when, coming into union with you, he sheds hot tears born of long separation.
t.1.11: Hearing that thunder, sweet to the ear, which has the power to make the earth fruitful and studded with mushrooms, they, the royal swans, longing for Mānasa and carrying as provisions bits of tender lotus-stalk shoots, will become your companions in the sky all the way to Kailāsa.
t.1.13: First, O cloud, hear from me as I describe the route suited to your journey; after that you will hear my message, a draught for the ears. Along that route you will travel, setting your foot upon the mountain peaks whenever you grow weary, and partaking of the light water of the streams whenever you grow thin.
t.1.14: Your vigor watched with mounting alarm by the artless wives of the Siddhas, who lift their faces wondering, 'Is the wind carrying off the mountain's peak?', fly up into the sky, facing north, from this place rich with sap-filled nicula trees, and on your path avoid the haughty blows of the massive trunks of the elephants of the quarters.
t.1.15: Before you, rising from the top of an anthill, a fragment of Ākhaṇḍala's bow is to be seen, as if in a mingling of the lustres of jewels; by it your dark body will attain exceeding loveliness, like that of Viṣṇu in a cowherd's guise through the peacock feather of shimmering splendour.
t.1.16: Thinking, "The fruit of our tilling depends on you," the village women drink you in with eyes tender with affection and knowing the motions of the brows. Climb the upland field of Māla, fragrant from the fresh furrowing of the plough, then go a little to the west, and, moving swiftly, turn once more to the north.
t.1.18: When you, colored like a glossy braid of hair, have climbed its summit, the mountain, its slopes covered with forest mangoes gleaming with ripened fruit, will surely attain a state worthy to be gazed upon by pairs of immortals: like a breast of the Earth, dark in the middle and pale over the rest of its expanse.
t.1.17: Mount Āmrakūṭa, rich in ridges, will gladly bear you upon his head, you who quenched the fire ravaging his forests with your downpours and who are worn by the weariness of the road. Even a lowly one does not turn away from a friend who has come to him for shelter, mindful of an earlier kindness; how much less one who is so lofty!
t.1.19: Having rested a moment in that bower enjoyed by the wives of the forest-dwellers, your pace made swifter by the release of your water, and having crossed the path beyond it, you will see the Revā spread in scattered streams over the rock-strewn foot of the Vindhya, like ornament painted in patterned streaks upon the body of an elephant.
t.1.20: O cloud, when you come before it weary from the road, the mountain Āmrakūṭa will honour you and bear you on its lofty peak. You in turn, moist with goodwill, should quench its summer fire with your downpour, for a kindness done to the great bears fruit without delay.
t.1.21: Having shed your rain, take up her water, scented with the pungent ichor of wild elephants, its current checked by thickets of jambū trees, and go on. Then, O cloud, solid within, you cannot be tossed about by the wind, for all that is empty is light, while fullness makes for weight.
t.1.22: Having seen the nīpa, green and tawny with its half-grown filaments, and having eaten the kandalī plants along the marshy banks, their first buds just appearing, and having breathed in the earth's richly fragrant scent in the forests, those sāraṅgas, shedding drops of water, will point out the path.
t.1.24: Friend, though you wish to go swiftly for the sake of my beloved, I foresee delay for you on mountain after mountain fragrant with kakubha blossoms, where the white-eyed peacocks, their eyes brimming with tears, will turn their cries into a welcome for you. Therefore, pressing past them, may you somehow resolve to go on quickly.
t.1.25: When you draw near, the Daśārṇas will become a land whose garden hedges are pale with ketaka blossoms bursting open at their tips, whose village shrine-trees are crowded with the nest-building of house-crows, and whose forest borders are dark with ripened jambū fruit, a land where the haṃsas stay only a few days.
t.1.28: Having rested, go on, sprinkling with fresh drops of water the clusters of jasmine buds in the gardens that grow along the banks of the forest rivers, and, by granting them shade, becoming for a moment acquainted with the faces of the flower-gathering women, whose ear-lotuses have wilted from the chafing as they wipe the sweat from their cheeks.
t.1.30: On your way, meeting the Nirvindhyā, whose girdle-string is the row of birds crying out as her waves toss, and who glides along with a lovely, faltering gait, become filled within with her waters, you who appear above her whirlpools laid bare. For playful coquetry is a woman's first declaration of love to her beloved.
t.1.34: In that city, seeing displayed in the markets by the crore necklaces with tremulous central gems, lustrous pearls, conches and oyster shells, emeralds dark as young grass with sprouts of upward-streaming rays, and pieces of coral, the oceans are perceived as having nothing but their water left.
t.1.37: Gazed upon reverently by the Gaṇas, who think, “This is the hue of our master’s throat,” you should go to the holy abode of Caṇḍīśvara, guru of the three worlds, whose gardens are stirred by breezes from the Gandhavatī, fragrant with the pollen of blue lotuses and scented by the bathing of young women absorbed in water-play.
t.1.40: Then, at the start of his dance, settle in a ring high upon the forest of Paśupati's tree-like arms, bearing the evening glow red as fresh japā flowers, and take away his wish for the wet elephant hide, while Bhavānī, her alarm calmed and her eyes grown still, beholds your devotion.
t.1.43: At that hour lovers must wipe away the tears of women wronged by their faithlessness, so quickly leave the path of the Sun. He too has returned to take the dewdrop tears from the lotus face of the lotus-pond, and he would grow fiercely resentful toward you if you blocked his rays.
t.1.46: As you seek to approach Mount Devagiri, a cool wind will blow gently for you, delightful with the scent of the earth that breathes forth under your showers, drunk in by elephants with a pleasing sound through the hollows of their trunks, and ripening the wild figs of the forests.
t.1.48: Then, with your thunderings made deep by echoing among the mountains, you should set dancing that peacock of Pāvaki, the corners of whose eyes are washed bright by the radiance of the moon on Hara's head, and whose fallen feather, ringed with circles of light, Bhavānī out of love for her son places upon her ear beside a blue lotus petal.
t.1.50: When you, thief of the hue of Śārṅgin, bend low to drink the water of that river, the beings who move through the sky, lowering their gaze, will surely behold its current, broad yet slender because of the distance, as a single string of pearls of the Earth with a large sapphire at its center.
t.1.52: Then, entering the land of Brahmāvarta with your shadow, you should visit that field of the Kurus, which bears witness to the great battle of the warriors, where the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow showered the faces of princes with hundreds of sharp arrows, just as you shower lotuses with falling torrents of rain.
t.1.53: Turning away from battle out of love for his kinsmen, the plough-bearer Balarāma gave up his beloved wine, whose flavor he cherished and which bore the reflection of Revatī's eyes, and resorted to the waters of the Sarasvatī. Gentle one, when you too have partaken of those waters, you will become pure within, dark in color alone.
t.1.55: If you, like a celestial elephant with your hind half hanging in the sky, should resolve to drink her slanting water, clear and bright as pure crystal, then, with your shadow at once gliding upon her stream, she would look as lovely as if she had met the Yamunā at an unexpected place.
t.1.56: Having reached the very source of that river, the mountain white with snows, whose rocks are perfumed by the musk of the deer that sit there, and settling on its peak to dispel the weariness of your journey, you will display a radiant beauty comparable to the mud thrown up by the bull of the Three-Eyed God.
t.1.58: Should the śarabhas there, reckless in their furious springing, suddenly leap at you, who have kept out of their way, only to shatter their own limbs, you should scatter them with a tumultuous downpour of hailstones; for who would not become an object of scorn when their efforts are undertaken in vain?
t.1.60: The bamboos, filled by the winds, sound sweetly; the victory over Tripura is sung by impassioned Kiṃnarīs; if your thunder should resound in the caves like a drum, then surely the whole purpose of Paśupati's concert will be fulfilled there.
t.1.61: Having passed beyond those many wondrous sights along the slopes of the Snow Mountain, you should travel toward the northern quarter through the Krauñca pass, the gateway of the swans and the path of Bhṛgupati's fame. Going obliquely, splendid in your stretched-out length and dark, you will seem like the foot of Viṣṇu lifted high to subdue Bali.
t.1.62: And going higher, you should become the guest of Kailāsa, mirror of the celestial women, the joints of whose slopes were loosened by the arms of Daśamukha; it stands spreading across the sky with its lofty peaks, white as kumuda lilies, like the loud laughter of Tryambaka heaped up day after day.
t.1.63: When you, gleaming like glossy crushed collyrium, have come to its slope, I foresee that the beauty of that mountain, white as a freshly cut section of an elephant's tusk, will be a sight to be gazed upon with unblinking eyes, like that of Halabhṛt when a dark-blue garment is draped upon his shoulder.
t.1.64: And if on that pleasure-mountain Gaurī should wander on foot, her hand held by Śambhu, who has laid aside his serpent-bracelet, then you, going on ahead, your body shaped into a succession of tiers and the flood of waters within you held still, become a stairway for her to climb the jewelled slopes.
t.1.65: There the young celestial women will surely make you into a shower-house of jetting streams, your water released by the striking of the diamonds on their bracelets. If, friend, you, caught by them in the hot season, find no release from them, frighten those playful women with thunderings harsh to the ear.
t.1.67: O you who roam at will, once you have seen Alakā resting on his lap as on a lover's, her silken garment, the Gaṅgā, slipping down, you cannot fail to recognize her. In your season, with her lofty palaces, she bears a mass of clouds pouring out water, as a passionate woman wears her locks braided with nets of pearls.
t.2.3: There the trees, ever in flower, hum with maddened bees; the lotus-ponds, ever full of lotuses, wear girdles woven of rows of geese; the peacocks of that realm, their tails ever gleaming, lift their throats eagerly in cries; and the evenings, ever moonlit, are lovely, for the reign of darkness has been banished.
t.2.6: There, fanned by breezes cooled by the waters of the Mandākinī, their heat kept off by the shade of the mandāra trees growing along her banks, maidens courted by the immortals play at a game with jewels that must be searched for, hidden by fistfuls of golden sand thrown over them.
t.2.9: There, at midnight, moonstones hanging in nets of threads, struck by moonbeams made bright once you no longer block them, trickle clear drops of water and dispel the bodily weariness born of lovemaking in women whose embraces in their dearest lovers' arms have just been loosened.
t.2.12: In that city a single wish-granting tree brings forth every adornment women need: bright-colored garments, wine skilled in teaching the eyes their playful glances, bursting blossoms together with tender shoots, ornaments of every kind, and the red lac-dye fit for the lotus feet to tread on.
t.2.15: There, to the north of the palace of the Lord of Wealth, stands our house, recognizable from afar by its arched gateway, lovely as the bow of the Lord of the Gods. Near it grows a young mandāra tree, reared by my beloved as if it were her own son, its boughs bent low with clusters of blossoms within reach of the hand.
t.2.17: On the bank of that pond stands a pleasure-hill, its summit fashioned of lovely sapphires, delightful to behold with its ring of golden plantain trees; thinking, 'it is dear to my wife,' O friend, I look upon you with lightning flickering at your edges and, with an anxious heart, remember that very hill.
t.2.20: Good friend, keep these signs in your heart, and you will recognize it by them and by the conch and the lotus painted beside the door. Surely the house now has a faded luster because of my separation, for when the sun is gone the lotus does not keep its own beauty.
t.2.22: Slender, youthful, with teeth like jasmine buds and a lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit, slim at the waist, with eyes like a startled doe's and a deep navel, slow in gait from the weight of her hips and bending a little under her breasts, she who dwells there must be the Creator's very first creation in the realm of young women.
t.2.24: Surely the face of my beloved, its eyes swollen from violent weeping, its lower lip discolored by the heat of her sighs, resting on her hand and only partly visible because of her hanging locks, bears the wretchedness of the moon whose radiance is dimmed as you follow upon it.
t.2.27: Or she will be setting out on the ground, counting them with flowers laid at the threshold, the months that remain of the term fixed on the day of our parting, or savoring a union begun only within her heart; for such, as a rule, are the diversions of women separated from their beloveds.
t.2.30: Out of former love her eye went toward the moon's rays, cool with nectar, that had entered through the lattice window, and it turned back again just as quickly. Out of grief she covers it with lashes heavy with tears, neither awake nor asleep, like a land-lotus on a cloudy day.
t.2.35: When you draw near, I suspect that the eye of the doe-eyed one, its sidelong glances checked by her locks, bare of the gloss of collyrium, and, since she has given up wine, having forgotten the play of its brows, will throb in its upper part and take on the likeness of the beauty of a blue water-lily trembling as fish stir the water.
t.2.39: O you whose husband lives, know me to be the cloud, your husband's dear friend, come to your side bearing his messages laid up in my heart. With deep and tender rumblings I speed along the road the weary bands of travelers far from home, eager to loosen the braided hair of their women.
t.2.42: Dwelling far away, his path barred by hostile fate, he enters through those yearning imaginings your body with his own: your slender body with his wasted one, your burning body with his intensely burning one, your tear-drenched body with his tearful one, your ceaselessly longing body with his longing one, your hot-sighing body with his that sighs still more deeply.
t.2.45: Having painted you on a rock with mineral colors, angry from love, when I wish to draw myself fallen at your feet, just then my sight is blotted out again and again by welling tears; cruel Fate does not tolerate the union of us two even in that.
t.2.46: O young one, though I am already wasted thin, the five-arrowed god torments me, far removed as I am from this face of yours, fragrant like earth sprinkled by showers. Consider, now that the hot season is at its end, how could the days pass for me, when the sunlight is scattered by dense clouds spreading wide and clinging to every quarter of the sky?
t.2.49: How might the three-watched night, with its long watches, be shortened as if to a moment? How might the day too, in all its phases, have only the faintest heat? Thus, O restless-eyed one, my heart, longing for what is hard to attain, has been left without refuge by the fiercely burning pangs of separation from you.
t.2.51: My curse will end when Śārṅgapāṇi rises from his serpent couch; pass the remaining four months with your eyes closed. Afterwards the two of us will enjoy each and every one of our heart's desires, multiplied by separation, through nights bright with the moonlight of full autumn.
t.2.53: Knowing from the giving of this token that I am well, O dark-eyed one, do not let gossip make you distrustful of me. People say that affections somehow wither away in separation; but in truth, through lack of enjoyment, their longing for the desired one swells, and they become a very heap of love.
t.1.26: Having gone to their royal capital, famed in all directions under the name Vidiśā, you will at once obtain the full, unimpaired fruit of being a lover, since you will drink the sweet water of the Vetravatī, with its rippling waves and made lovely by your thunder near her banks, as one drinks from a face with knitted brows.
t.1.23: Watching the cātakas skilled at catching raindrops, and counting and pointing out the cranes that have formed into rows, the Siddhas, on meeting you at the hour of thunder, will cherish the trembling embraces their beloved companions give them in sudden alarm.
t.1.27: There, for the sake of rest, you should stay upon the mountain called Nīcais, which, with its kadambas in full bloom, seems to bristle with delight at your touch. Through its rock-hewn chambers breathing out the fragrance of love-play with lovely women, it proclaims the unbridled youth of the townsmen.
t.1.29: Though the road is a detour for you as you set out toward the northern quarter, do not turn away from the loving embrace of the palace terraces of Ujjayinī; if you do not delight there in the eyes of the city's women, with their tremulous corners, startled by the flashing of your lightning-garlands, you have been cheated.
t.1.31: When you have passed beyond her, the Sindhu, her thinned waters gathered into a single braid, pale in hue from the withered leaves dropping from the trees that grow on her banks, reveals by her state of separation your good fortune, O fortunate one; the means by which she may cast off her thinness must be brought about by you alone.
t.1.32: Having reached the Avantis, where the village elders are well versed in the tales of Udayana, approach the city I mentioned before, Viśālā, vast in splendor, as if it were a single radiant fragment carried off from heaven by the remaining merits of heaven-dwellers who had come down to earth when the fruit of their good deeds had grown small.
t.1.33: There, at daybreak, the breeze of the Śiprā carries far the shrill cries of the cranes, sweet and indistinct with passion, and is tinged by its friendship with the fragrance of opening lotuses. Pleasant to the limbs, it takes away the women's weariness after lovemaking, like a dearest lover who flatters them with entreating words.
t.1.35: “Here the king of Vatsa carried off Pradyota’s beloved daughter; here stood that same king’s golden grove of palm trees; here, they say, the elephant Nalagiri, in his pride, tore up his post and ran wild.” With such tales the knowledgeable people there entertain their visiting kinsmen.
t.1.36: Your body swelled by the smoke of hair-perfuming incense pouring out through the lattice windows, and offered the gift of a dance by the household peacocks out of fondness for a kinsman, you should shed the weariness of your journey in her mansions, fragrant with flowers and marked with the red lac from the feet of graceful women, as you gaze upon their splendor.
t.1.38: O cloud, even if you reach Mahākāla at some other time, you must stay there until the sun passes beyond the range of sight. By serving as the praiseworthy drum for the evening offering of Śūlin, you will gain the full fruit of your deep, rumbling thunder.
t.1.39: There the courtesans, their girdles jingling with the placing of their feet, their hands wearied by the chowries playfully waved, whose handles are inlaid with the lustre of jewels, will, on receiving from you the first drops of rain so soothing to their nail-marks, cast upon you sidelong glances long as a line of bees.
t.1.41: There at night, when the light on the royal highway is blocked by a darkness so thick that only a needle could pierce it, show the ground to the women going to their lovers' dwellings with your lightning, glowing like a streak of gold on a touchstone. But do not be loud with the release of rain and thunder, for they are timid.
t.1.42: Having spent that night on the roof-turret of some mansion where doves lie asleep, your consort the lightning wearied from her long play, you should, once the sun is seen, travel on again over the remainder of the road; for those who have taken upon themselves the business of friends surely do not grow slack.
t.1.44: Into the water of the river Gambhīrā, clear as a serene mind, even your shadow-self, lovely by nature, will gain entry. Therefore you ought not, out of steadfast reserve, make fruitless her glances, white as night-lotuses, which are the leaps of her darting śaphara fish.
t.1.45: Once you have carried off her blue garment of water, which has slipped from the hips of her banks and is held, as if by her hand, by the reed branches it has reached, your departure, friend, as you hang low over her, will come about only with difficulty; for who that has known the taste of pleasure is able to leave a woman whose loins are laid bare?
t.1.47: There, transforming yourself into a cloud of flowers, may you bathe Skanda, who dwells there constantly, with showers of blossoms moistened by the waters of the heavenly Gaṅgā; for he is that radiance surpassing the sun, gathered by the bearer of the new moon into the mouth of the fire-god for the protection of Vāsava's armies.
t.1.49: Having worshipped this god born in the reed-thicket, travel on, your path left clear by Siddha couples bearing lutes who fear the drops of water, and stoop low to honor the fame of Rantideva, born of the sacrifice of Surabhi's daughters, which has been transformed on earth into the body of a stream.
t.1.51: Having crossed her, go on, making your own form the object of the eager eyes of the women of Daśapura, women versed in the playful arching of their creeper-like brows, whose dark and bright glances flash upward as they lift their lashes, and who steal the beauty of bees that chase a tossed kunda flower.
t.1.54: From there you should go on to Kanakhala, to the daughter of Jahnu, descended from the king of mountains, a flight of stairs to heaven for the sons of Sagara. As if laughing with her foam at the frown formed on Gaurī's face, she seized Śambhu by the hair, her wave-hands clinging to the moon.
t.1.57: If, when the wind blows, a forest fire born of the rubbing together of sarala-tree trunks should trouble that mountain, its sparks singeing the masses of the yak-cows' tail-hair, you ought to quench it fully with thousands of streams of water, for the wealth of the noblest bears fruit in relieving the suffering of those in distress.
t.1.59: There, bowed low in devotion, you should circle the footprint of the half-moon-crested one, clearly visible upon the rock and ever heaped with offerings by the Siddhas; for when it has been seen, the faithful, their sins shaken off, become fit after the falling away of the body to attain the abiding station of his Gaṇas.
t.1.66: Drinking the water of Mānasa, which gives birth to golden lotuses, granting Airāvata at will the brief delight of a veil across his face, and with your winds shaking the tender shoots of the wish-granting trees as if they were silken garments, may you enjoy that lord of mountains with the many playful movements of a cloud.
t.2.1: There, the palaces are fully able to rival you through their many distinctive features: you set graceful women trembling, while they hold lovely women; you bear the rainbow, while they are adorned with paintings; your thunder is deep and resonant, while their drums are struck for music; you carry water within, while their floors are made of jewels; and you are lofty, while their tops lick the clouds.
t.2.2: There the women hold a play-lotus in the hand and wear young kunda blossoms woven into their locks; the beauty of their faces is made pale with the pollen of lodhra flowers. In their braided hair they set fresh kuravaka, on the ear a lovely śirīṣa, and in the parting of the hair the nīpa blossom born of your coming.
t.2.4: There, where tears spring to the eyes from joy and from no other cause, there is no anguish but that born of the flower-arrowed god of love, which union with the beloved can cure. No separation arises except from lovers' quarrels, and for the lords of wealth there is surely no age other than youth.
t.2.5: There the Yakṣas, accompanied by the most excellent women, come to the terraces of their mansions made of white gems, adorned with flowers formed by the reflections of the stars, and enjoy the wine born of the wish-granting tree, whose fruit is love's delight, while drums deep-toned like your thunder are softly beaten.
t.2.8: In that city, clouds like you, led by their guide the ever-moving wind onto the topmost floors of its palaces, at once spoil the paintings there with drops of water, and then, as if seized by fear, slip out through the lattice windows, shredded into tatters, skilled at mimicking the puffs of smoke.
t.2.7: There, when lovers, their hands restless with passion, pull away the silken garments of the bimba-lipped women, already loosened by the untying of the waist-knot, the handful of powder flung by those women, bewildered with shame, is thrown in vain, for though it strikes the jewel-lamps with their tall flames full in front, it cannot put them out.
t.2.10: There, lovers with inexhaustible treasures stored within their mansions, accompanied by the foremost courtesans among the celestial women and absorbed in conversation, daily enjoy the outer garden called Vaibhrāja, together with sweet-throated Kiṃnaras who sing aloud the glory of the Lord of Wealth.
t.2.11: There, at the rising of the sun, the nightly path of the amorous women is betrayed by mandāra flowers fallen from their locks through the trembling of their hurried gait, by leaf-shaped ornaments and golden lotuses slipped from their ears, by nets of pearls, and by necklaces whose strings snapped against the swell of their breasts.
t.2.13: There the horses, dark as leaves, rival the steeds of the Sun; the elephants, lofty as mountains, rain ichor from their rut like you; and the foremost warriors, who stood in battle against Daśamukha, bear scars from the Candrahāsa sword that put the splendor of ornaments to shame.
t.2.14: Knowing that the god who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth dwells there in person, Manmatha, out of fear, mostly does not carry his bow strung with bees; his work is accomplished by the coquetries of clever women alone, whose glances, darted with knitted brows, never miss their targets, the lovers.
t.2.16: And in it there is a pond whose flight of steps is laid with slabs of emerald, covered with full-blown golden lotuses on stalks of glossy beryl; the swans who have made their dwelling in its water, free from sorrow, will not pine for nearby Lake Mānasa even when they see you.
t.2.18: Here, close to the mādhavī bower with its hedge of kuravaka, stand a red aśoka with trembling young shoots and a lovely kesara. The one, like me, longs for the left foot of your friend; the other, under the pretext of its flowering-craving, yearns for the wine of her mouth.
t.2.19: And in the midst of them stands a golden perching-pole topped with a crystal slab, bound at its base with gems that gleam like young bamboo, on which, at the close of day, sits your friend the blue-throated peacock, made to dance by my beloved with clapping hands made lovely by tinkling bracelets.
t.2.21: Swiftly taking on the slender form of a young elephant so that you may descend quickly, and seated on the lovely summit of the pleasure-hill I spoke of before, you should cast into the house the glance of your lightning's flash, its light dimmed little by little, like the flickering play of a row of fireflies.
t.2.23: Know her, sparing of speech, to be my second life, alone like a female cakravāka while I, her companion, am far away; I think that the young woman, her longing grown intense as these heavy days pass, has become changed in form, like a lotus plant blighted by the frost.
t.2.25: She falls first upon your sight, either busy with the offerings, or drawing my likeness, wasted by separation, as her heart imagines it, or asking the sweet-voiced myna in its cage, “Do you remember our master, O tender one? For you were his darling.”
t.2.26: Or, gentle one, you will find her with her vīṇā laid on her lap in its soiled garment, longing to sing aloud a song whose words she has composed around my name. Having somehow wiped dry the string wet with the tears of her eyes, she forgets again and again the modulation, though she herself had composed it.
t.2.28: By day, while she is occupied with tasks, separation may not torment her so; but at night, I fear, your friend suffers heavier grief with nothing to divert her. So that you may comfort her with my messages, look upon that virtuous one at midnight, sleepless and lying on the bare ground, as you stand at the window of the mansion.
t.2.29: You will see her wasted with anguish, lying on one side upon her bed of separation, like the slender form of the cool-rayed moon with only a single digit left, low on the eastern horizon. With hot tears she drags through that very night, now made long by separation, which once, spent with me in love-play as we desired, passed like a single moment.
t.2.31: You will surely find her blowing aside, with sighs that torment the tender bud of her lower lip, the lock of hair that hangs down to her cheek, rough from bathing in plain water, and longing for sleep, though the welling flood of tears leaves it no room, wondering how union with me might come to her, even if only born of a dream.
t.2.32: She, with her hand whose nails are uncut, again and again pushes away from the curve of her cheek the single braid, hard, uneven and painful to the touch: that lock which was bound on the first day of our separation, its garland cast aside, and which I am to unbind at the end of the curse, when my grief has melted away.
t.2.33: That frail woman, bearing her delicate body stripped of its ornaments and laid again and again, with grievous pain, upon the lap of her bed, will surely make even you shed tears of fresh water; for, as a rule, everyone whose inner self is tender becomes compassionate.
t.2.34: I know that your friend's heart is filled with love for me; for this reason I imagine her to be in such a state in this first separation. It is surely not the conceit of thinking myself fortunate that makes me talkative; all that I have said, brother, you will soon see with your own eyes.
t.2.36: And her left thigh, now bereft of the marks of my nails and made by the course of fate to give up its long-familiar net of pearls, that thigh, pale as the stem of a fresh plantain and accustomed at the close of love's enjoyment to the soothing strokes of my hands, will begin to quiver.
t.2.37: At that time, O cloud, if she should be enjoying the bliss of sleep, wait beside her, holding back your thunder, and be patient for just one watch of the night. Otherwise her close embrace of me, her lover somehow found in a dream, might suddenly come undone, the knot of her creeper-like arms slipping from my neck.
t.2.38: Having roused her with a breeze cooled by your own fine droplets of water, so that she revives together with the fresh clusters of mālatī buds, keep your lightning hidden within you and, steady, begin to speak with words of thunder to that proud lady as she gazes with unmoving eyes at the window where you rest.
t.2.40: When you have spoken thus, she, like Maithilī turning eagerly toward the son of the Wind, will look up at you with a heart swelling with longing, and having welcomed you with honor, will listen attentively to what follows, gentle one; for to women, news of a beloved brought by a friend is only a little less than union itself.
t.2.41: O long-lived one, at my word and to do a kindness to yourself as well, you should speak to her thus: "Your companion, dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, still alive though parted from you, asks, O helpless one, after your well-being; for to living beings, to whom misfortunes come so easily, this is the very first thing to be said."
t.2.43: He who, out of longing to touch your face, used to be eager to whisper in your ear before your friends even what might well have been spoken aloud, he, now passed beyond the range of hearing and unseen by your eyes, speaks to you through my mouth these words, composed by longing.
t.2.44: In the śyāmā creepers I see your body, in the glances of startled does your gaze, in the moon the radiance of your face, in the heavy plumes of peacocks your hair, and in the slender ripples of rivers the playful arching of your brows. But alas, O fierce one, nowhere in any single thing is there a likeness of you.
t.2.48: O virtuous one, I embrace those winds from the snowy mountain which, having just burst open the leaf-bud sheaths of the devadāru trees and grown fragrant with the flow of their sap, have set out toward the south, thinking that perhaps they may have touched your body before.
t.2.47: When the deities of the woodland see me stretching my arms out into empty space to clasp you in a fierce embrace, you whom I have somehow found in visions of my dreams, surely it is not seldom that their tear-drops, large as pearls, fall upon the tender shoots of the trees.
t.2.50: Indeed, reflecting much upon myself, I sustain myself by my own strength; therefore, O fair one, do not you too fall into utter despair. To whom has happiness come without end, or sorrow absolutely? One's condition goes down and goes up in the manner of a wheel's rim.
t.2.52: And he said further: Once, long ago, as you lay in bed clinging to my neck, you fell asleep and then woke suddenly, weeping aloud for some reason; and when I asked you again and again, you told me with a hidden laugh, 'Rogue, I saw you in a dream making love to some other woman!'
t.2.54: Having thus consoled your friend, whose grief is fierce in this first separation, return swiftly from the mountain whose peaks are torn up by the bull of the Three-Eyed One. With her words, which send a token of recognition and news of her well-being, you should sustain my life too, which droops like a jasmine blossom at dawn.
t.2.55: I trust, gentle friend, that you have resolved to perform this friendly service for me; I surely do not take your grave silence as a refusal. Even without a sound you give water to the cātaka birds when they beg for it, for the only answer the good give to those who entreat them is to accomplish what they desire.
